Left atrium.description: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the four pulmonary veins and pumps it through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. Its thin back wall lies in front of the oesophagus, and the left auricle is a small pouch that curls forward beside the pulmonary trunk. The interatrial septum separates it from the right atrium and carries the fossa ovalis, a remnant of the fetal foramen ovale.
clinical: Atrial fibrillation and clots

In atrial fibrillation the atria quiver instead of contracting properly, and blood pools in the left auricle. Clots that form there can break loose and cause a stroke, which is why many patients take anticoagulant drugs.
Patent foramen ovale

The fetal opening between the atria normally closes after birth, but in some adults a gap stays partly open. It is often harmless, but it can let a clot pass from the right side of the heart to the left.

Left ventricle.description: The left ventricle is the thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood out through the aortic valve to the whole body. Its wall is several times thicker than the right ventricle's, and it forms the apex of the heart, the front and side walls, and the interventricular septum. Most of it is supplied by the left anterior descending artery (front wall, septum and apex) and the circumflex artery (side wall), with the right coronary artery supplying the inferior wall in most people.
clinical: Heart attack territories

Each territory of the left ventricle is supplied mainly by one coronary artery. Blockage of the LAD damages the front wall and septum, the right coronary artery usually damages the inferior wall, and the circumflex artery damages the lateral wall.
Ventricular septal defect

A hole in the interventricular septum, one of the most common congenital heart defects, lets blood pass from the left ventricle into the right. Small defects often close on their own, while large ones overload the lungs with extra blood.

Right atrium.description: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, then pumps it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Its back wall is smooth where the venae cavae enter, while its free side is ridged by pectinate muscles that run from the crista terminalis toward the right auricle, a broad pouch that overlaps the aortic root. The sinoatrial node sits near the upper end of the crista terminalis.
clinical: Atrial flutter

The typical flutter circuit runs around the tricuspid valve inside the right atrium. Ablation of the isthmus between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid ring is a standard, usually curative treatment.

Right ventricle.description: The right ventricle receives blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve and pumps it through a smooth outflow tract, the infundibulum, and the pulmonary valve into the lungs. Its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's, and its front and lower walls are supplied mainly by branches of the right coronary artery. Three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior and septal) anchor the chordae that stop the tricuspid leaflets prolapsing into the right atrium during systole.
clinical: Right ventricular infarction

A blocked right coronary artery often damages the right ventricle as well as the inferior wall of the left ventricle. A weakened right ventricle may cause a sudden fall in blood pressure, so treatment must take it into account.
Pulmonary hypertension
Long-standing high pressure in the lung circulation, for example from chronic lung disease, makes the right ventricle thicken to pump harder and eventually dilate and fail.

Coronary arteries.description: The coronary arteries leave the aortic root just above the aortic valve and run over the heart surface to supply the heart muscle itself. The left main artery divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries, while the right coronary artery supplies the right heart and usually the posterior descending artery. Blockage of any of these arteries starves the muscle beyond it and can cause a heart attack.
clinical: Coronary artery disease

Atherosclerotic plaques narrow the coronary arteries, often the LAD, and limit blood flow, especially during exercise. If a plaque ruptures and blocks the artery, the area it supplies undergoes infarction.
Heart block in inferior infarcts
The AV nodal artery usually comes from the right coronary artery, so an inferior infarct can damage the AV node and cause heart block.
Coronary sinus and a left superior vena cava

The coronary sinus is the main drain of the cardiac veins, opening into the right atrium. In an uncommon persistent left superior vena cava, a vein from the left side of the chest drains into it, so the sinus looks enlarged on imaging.
Pacing the left ventricle

Pacing leads for cardiac resynchronisation are often threaded through the coronary sinus into a lateral cardiac vein to pace the left ventricle. This is why the anatomy of the coronary sinus matters before device placement.

Aorta and arch branches.description: The aorta leaves the left ventricle through the aortic valve, rises as the ascending aorta, arches over the left pulmonary artery and left main bronchus, and continues down the chest as the descending aorta. The arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, which supply the head, neck and arms.
clinical: Aortic dissection

A tear in the inner wall of the aorta lets blood split the layers of the wall. A dissection of the ascending aorta (type A) is a surgical emergency because it can rupture or block branches such as the coronary arteries.
Coarctation of the aorta

A narrowing of the aorta, usually just beyond the left subclavian artery, raises blood pressure in the arms and reduces flow to the legs. Doctors look for it by comparing blood pressure in the arms with that in the legs.

Venae cavae and brachiocephalic veins.description: The superior vena cava is formed where the two brachiocephalic veins join, and it carries blood from the head, neck and arms into the top of the right atrium. The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm and returns blood from the lower body to the bottom of the right atrium. The left brachiocephalic vein crosses in front of the arch branches to reach the right side.
clinical: Superior vena cava syndrome
Blockage of the superior vena cava, often by a lung tumour or enlarged lymph nodes, causes swelling of the face, neck and arms with distended veins over the chest. It needs urgent treatment.
Central venous lines
Central venous catheters are often advanced through the superior vena cava, with the tip ideally near its junction with the right atrium. That is why the tip position is checked on an X-ray.
Pulmonary veins and atrial fibrillation
Rapid electrical firing from muscle sleeves that extend onto the pulmonary veins often starts atrial fibrillation. Catheter ablation that isolates these veins is a common treatment.
Pulmonary embolism

A clot, usually from a deep vein in the leg, can lodge in a pulmonary artery and block blood flow to part of the lung. A very large clot at the bifurcation can block both pulmonary arteries and cause sudden collapse.
Patent ductus arteriosus

The ductus arteriosus is a fetal shunt between the pulmonary artery and the aorta that normally closes soon after birth; the ligamentum arteriosum is its remnant. If it stays open, it causes a continuous 'machinery' murmur and extra blood flow to the lungs.
Aortic stenosis

Calcium deposits stiffen and narrow the aortic valve, so the left ventricle must work harder. The classic murmur is a harsh systolic sound heard at the upper right sternal edge that may radiate to the neck.
Bicuspid aortic valve
Some people are born with two cusps instead of three. This is the most common congenital valve anomaly, and it often leads to stenosis or regurgitation and is linked to dilatation of the aorta.

Valve annuli (fibrous rings).description: Rings of dense fibrous tissue surround the mitral and tricuspid openings. They give the atrioventricular valves their shape and anchor the leaflets, and they stretch when the chambers dilate, which can let blood leak back.
clinical: Functional mitral regurgitation
When the left ventricle or left atrium enlarges, the mitral ring widens and the leaflets no longer meet, so blood leaks back even though the valve leaflets are healthy.
Functional tricuspid regurgitation
Right ventricular dilatation, for example from pulmonary hypertension or left heart failure, stretches the tricuspid ring so the leaflets fail to close.
Mitral valve prolapse
In prolapse the leaflets bulge back into the left atrium during systole. The posterior leaflet is most often involved, and the condition can cause a mid-systolic click and regurgitation.
Mitral stenosis
The leaflets thicken and fuse, classically after rheumatic fever, which narrows the opening and enlarges the left atrium. It produces a rumbling diastolic murmur best heard at the apex.
Ruptured chordae

The chordae stop the leaflets prolapsing into the atrium during systole. If one ruptures, for example after a heart attack, endocarditis or in prolapse, sudden severe mitral regurgitation and breathlessness can follow.

Papillary muscles.description: Papillary muscles are cone-shaped muscles arising from the ventricular wall. The chordae tendineae attach to their tips, so they hold the valve leaflets closed and stop them prolapsing into the atria during systole. The left ventricle has two (anterolateral and posteromedial) and the right ventricle has three (anterior, posterior and septal).
clinical: Papillary muscle rupture

The posteromedial papillary muscle usually has a single blood supply from the posterior descending artery, so an inferior infarct can cause it to rupture. This produces sudden severe mitral regurgitation and is a surgical emergency.
Ischaemic mitral regurgitation
If a papillary muscle is weakened by ischaemia, or the ventricle dilates, it pulls the leaflets apart so they cannot close fully, and blood leaks back into the atrium.
Pulmonary stenosis
Usually congenital, a narrowed pulmonary valve makes the right ventricle work harder and thicken. It causes a systolic ejection murmur heard at the upper left sternal edge.
Ebstein anomaly

In this congenital malformation the septal and posterior leaflets are displaced down toward the apex, and the upper part of the right ventricle becomes thin and works like part of the atrium. The result is tricuspid regurgitation and an enlarged right atrium.
Tricuspid valve endocarditis
Infection of the tricuspid valve is especially common in people who inject drugs, and fragments of infected vegetation can lodge in the lungs as septic emboli.

Conduction system.description: The conduction system generates and carries the heartbeat. The sinoatrial node in the right atrium sets the rhythm, and the impulse passes through the atrioventricular (AV) node and bundle of His, then down both bundle branches into the Purkinje fibres, which make the ventricles contract from the apex upward.
clinical: Heart block
If the AV node or His bundle is damaged, impulses are slowed or blocked, so the ventricles beat more slowly or on their own rhythm. A pacemaker is often needed to keep a safe rate.
Bundle branch block
A block in the right or left bundle branch makes one ventricle depolarise late, which widens the QRS complex on the ECG.

Atrial pathways.description: Atrial pathways are tracts of atrial muscle that carry the impulse from the sinoatrial node toward the atrioventricular node. The anterior, middle and posterior internodal pathways run to the AV node, and Bachmann bundle carries the impulse across the roof of the atria into the left atrium so that both atria contract almost together.
clinical: Atrial fibrillation

In atrial fibrillation chaotic electrical impulses spread across the atria, so they quiver instead of contracting in an organised way. The irregular impulses reaching the AV node make the heartbeat irregular.
Interatrial block
Slow conduction through Bachmann bundle is thought to cause interatrial block, in which the P wave lasts 120 ms or more. It is linked to a higher risk of atrial fibrillation.
Accessory pathways

The fibrous skeleton normally insulates the atrial muscle from the ventricular muscle, so the AV node is the only route for impulses. An extra muscle bridge across this barrier, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, lets impulses bypass the node and can cause fast rhythms.
Pericarditis

Inflammation of the pericardial layers, often after a viral infection or heart attack, causes sharp chest pain that eases when the patient sits forward. A friction rub may be heard through a stethoscope.
Cardiac tamponade

Fluid collecting in the pericardial cavity can compress the heart. Because the fibrous pericardium stretches very little, a rapid build-up of even moderate fluid can stop the heart filling and cause shock.

Diaphragm.description: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle and forms the floor of the chest cavity. Its central tendon is fused with the fibrous pericardium, which is why the heart rests on the diaphragm and why the lower wall of the left ventricle is called diaphragmatic.
clinical: Pericardial pain felt in the shoulder
The phrenic nerve supplies both the diaphragm and the pericardium, so irritation of the pericardium can be felt as pain in the shoulder, neck or upper abdomen.

Wall block (3x).description: This enlarged cross-section of the heart wall runs from the outside in: the fibrous and serous pericardium around the pericardial cavity, the epicardium with its coronary vessels and fat, the thick myocardium, and the endocardium that lines the chamber and touches the blood. Trabeculae carneae, the muscular ridges inside the ventricle, and Purkinje fibres are also included.
clinical: Heart attack and scarring
Cardiac muscle that loses its blood supply dies, and adult heart muscle regenerates very poorly, so the area heals with scar tissue.
Infective endocarditis
Bacteria can settle on the endocardium, usually over a heart valve, and form growths called vegetations that may break off as emboli.

Atrial wall block (3x).description: This enlarged cross-section of the right atrial wall shows thin atrial muscle, with smooth endocardium on the inside and epicardium on the outside. Inside the chamber, the crista terminalis and the pectinate muscles form muscular ridges, and the sinoatrial node lies near the top of the crista terminalis.
clinical: Sinus node disease
Disease of the sinoatrial node, near the top of the crista terminalis, can cause a slow heart rate or pauses, and a pacemaker is often needed.

parts.description: The interatrial septum is the thin wall of the heart that separates the right atrium from the left atrium. It is a sheet of fibrous tissue with a little muscle, lined on both sides by endocardium. Its central part carries the fossa ovalis, a shallow depression that is the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, the opening that let blood pass from right atrium to left before birth. Failure of this opening to close after birth leaves a patent (still open) foramen ovale.

The interventricular septum is the thick wall that separates the left ventricle from the right ventricle. Most of it is muscular, and it bulges towards the right ventricle because the left ventricle works at much higher pressure. Its small upper membranous part lies just below the aortic valve, and it is the usual site of a ventricular septal defect, a common congenital hole between the two ventricles.

The anterior wall of the left atrium is the front wall of the chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs, and it lies directly behind the root of the aorta. It is thin, and its inner surface is smooth because the ridged pectinate muscles are confined to the left auricle.

The posterior wall of the left atrium is the back wall of the chamber, lying directly in front of the oesophagus. The four pulmonary veins open into the back of the atrium, so this wall is where oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the heart. Because the oesophagus lies so close behind it, an enlarged left atrium can press on the oesophagus.

The left auricle, or left atrial appendage, is a small ear-shaped pouch that projects forward from the upper left part of the left atrium. It lies beside the pulmonary trunk, and its ridged inner surface is lined with pectinate muscles, unlike the smooth wall of the rest of the atrium. Blood can pool and clot inside it during atrial fibrillation, which is why it is the usual site of clot formation in that arrhythmia.

The anterior wall of the left ventricle is the front wall of the main pumping chamber on the left side of the heart. Its thick muscle is supplied mainly by the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, so a blockage of that artery typically causes an anterior heart attack. On a cut section, this wall is several times thicker than the right ventricle's, and its inner surface is ridged with trabeculae carneae.

The apex of the left ventricle is the rounded lower tip of the heart, where the walls of the left ventricle converge. It lies against the chest wall at about the fifth left intercostal space in the midclavicular line, which is where the apex beat, the impulse of each heartbeat, can be felt on examination. It is also the mitral area, the best place to listen with a stethoscope for the sounds of the mitral valve.

The inferior wall of the left ventricle is the lower surface of the chamber, which rests on the central tendon of the diaphragm. In most people it is supplied by the posterior descending artery, a branch of the right coronary artery, so a blockage there typically causes an inferior heart attack. It lies to the left of the posterior interventricular groove, which marks its boundary with the right ventricle on the lower surface of the heart.

The lateral wall of the left ventricle is the outer, left-facing wall of the chamber, and it forms the rounded left border of the heart. It lies against the left lung and the ribs, and it is supplied mainly by the circumflex artery through its obtuse marginal branches. A blockage of that supply causes a lateral heart attack, which shows changes in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 on the ECG.

The lateral wall of the right atrium is the outer, right-sided wall of the upper right heart chamber, and it forms much of the right border of the heart. Its inner surface is ridged with pectinate muscles, which run from the crista terminalis, a vertical muscular ridge, toward the right auricle. The smooth-walled posterior part of the atrium lies behind this ridge, so the crista terminalis is a useful landmark for recognising the lateral wall in a section.

The posterior wall of the right atrium is the smooth-walled back part of the chamber, where the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus open into it. It is smooth because it develops from the embryonic sinus venosus, and it is separated from the ridged front and side walls by the crista terminalis. The right pulmonary veins pass behind this wall on their way to the left atrium.

The right auricle, or right atrial appendage, is a small ear-shaped pouch that projects forward from the upper front of the right atrium. It overlaps the root of the aorta, and its inner surface is ridged with pectinate muscles, unlike the smooth back of the atrium. That ridged lining is a quick way to tell it apart from the smooth posterior wall when the heart is opened.

The anterior wall of the right ventricle is the front wall of the right-sided pumping chamber, lying directly behind the sternum and the costal cartilages. It forms most of the sternocostal (front) surface of the heart, and it is much thinner than the left ventricle's wall. It is supplied mainly by right coronary artery branches such as the right marginal artery, and its inner surface is coarsely ridged with trabeculae carneae.

The inferior wall of the right ventricle is the lower, diaphragmatic part of the right-sided chamber, lying on the central tendon of the diaphragm. It is supplied mainly by the right coronary artery and its posterior descending branch, so it can be damaged in an inferior heart attack when that artery is blocked. Its wall is thinner than the left ventricle's, and the posterior descending artery runs in the groove that separates it from the left ventricle.

The outflow tract of the right ventricle, also called the conus arteriosus or infundibulum, is the funnel-shaped upper part of the right ventricle that leads to the pulmonary trunk. Its wall is smooth because its muscle lacks the coarse trabeculae carneae found in the rest of the ventricle, which is a useful clue in a dissection. It ends at the pulmonary valve, and narrowing here, called infundibular stenosis, is one feature of tetralogy of Fallot.

The atrioventricular (AV) nodal artery is a small artery that supplies the AV node, the relay station that passes the electrical impulse from the atria to the ventricles. In most people it arises from the right coronary artery at the crux of the heart, where the atrioventricular and posterior interventricular grooves meet. Blockage of this artery can damage the node and cause heart block, a delay or failure of impulses reaching the ventricles.

The conus artery is a small branch that supplies the conus arteriosus, the smooth-walled outflow tract at the top of the right ventricle. It often arises as one of the first branches of the right coronary artery near the aortic root, although in some people it comes directly from the aorta. Its branches join a ring of vessels around the base of the pulmonary trunk, known as Vieussens' ring, which links it with the left coronary system.

The first anterior cardiac vein is one of the small veins that drain the front wall of the right ventricle. It crosses the right atrioventricular groove, the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle, and opens directly into the right atrium rather than into the coronary sinus. Because it bypasses the coronary sinus, it is a separate, direct route for returning blood from the heart muscle to the right atrium.

The first diagonal artery is an early branch of the left anterior descending artery that runs obliquely across the front wall of the left ventricle. It supplies the anterolateral wall, the part of the ventricle that faces the front and left chest wall. A blockage here can cause a heart attack of the front and side of the left ventricle, and the artery is recognised by its oblique course across the front of the heart.

The first obtuse marginal artery is the first branch of the circumflex artery, and it runs down the rounded left border of the heart, the obtuse margin. It supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle and runs beside the left marginal vein. A blockage in this artery can cause a heart attack of the lateral wall of the left ventricle.

The first septal perforator is one of several small branches of the left anterior descending artery that dive into the front of the interventricular septum, the thick muscular wall between the ventricles. It supplies the anterior part of the septum and helps to supply the conduction fibres that run in it. These branches leave the LAD at right angles and pass straight through the septum, which is why they are called perforators.

The great cardiac vein is the large vein that runs along the front of the heart, beside the left anterior descending artery. It begins near the apex and climbs the anterior interventricular groove, then curves left beside the circumflex artery in the atrioventricular groove. It becomes the coronary sinus where the oblique vein of the left atrium joins, and it drains the anterior left ventricle and septum.

A tributary of the great cardiac vein is a small vein that drains the anterior and anterolateral wall of the left ventricle and joins the main vein as it climbs beside the left anterior descending artery. It is short and thin-walled, and it is recognised as a small vessel entering the side of the great cardiac vein on the front of the heart. Its blood eventually reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus.

The anterior interventricular artery, usually called the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, is one of the two main branches of the left coronary artery. It runs down the anterior interventricular groove, the shallow groove on the front of the heart between the two ventricles, and reaches the apex. It supplies the front of both ventricles and the front two-thirds of the interventricular septum, so a blockage near its origin is a very serious heart attack.

The circumflex artery is one of the two main branches of the left coronary artery, and it runs to the left in the atrioventricular groove, the groove that encircles the heart where the atria meet the ventricles. It supplies the left atrium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle through its obtuse marginal branches. A blockage here can cause a lateral heart attack, and in a dissection the artery lies alongside the great cardiac vein in the left atrioventricular groove.

The left coronary artery, or left main stem, is the short, wide artery that leaves the left side of the aortic root just above the aortic valve. It divides almost at once into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries, and together these supply most of the left ventricle and the interventricular septum. Because so much muscle depends on this one short trunk, narrowing of the left main artery can be life-threatening.

The left marginal vein is a small vein that runs up the rounded left border of the heart, the obtuse margin, beside the obtuse marginal branch of the circumflex artery. It collects blood from the lateral wall of the left ventricle and empties into the great cardiac vein. Its course along the left border makes it easy to find by following the obtuse marginal artery in a dissection.

A tributary of the left marginal vein is a small vein that joins its parent along the left border of the heart and drains the lateral wall of the left ventricle. It is found by following the left marginal vein along the obtuse margin until the small branch enters from one side. Its blood passes through the left marginal vein into the great cardiac vein, and so reaches the coronary sinus and right atrium.

The middle cardiac vein runs up the back of the heart, in the posterior interventricular groove beside the posterior interventricular artery. It starts near the apex and ends in the coronary sinus close to its opening into the right atrium. It drains the posterior parts of both ventricles and of the septum.

A tributary of the middle cardiac vein is a small vein that drains the posterior and inferior walls of the ventricles and joins the main vein as it runs up the posterior interventricular groove. Because it is short and thin-walled, it is easily overlooked unless the middle cardiac vein is followed from the apex upwards. Its blood passes up the middle cardiac vein into the coronary sinus and then the right atrium.

The oblique vein of the left atrium, also called the vein of Marshall, is a small vein that runs down the back wall of the left atrium and drains into the coronary sinus. It is a remnant of the embryonic left common cardinal vein and joins the left-hand end of the coronary sinus. In some people a persistent left superior vena cava is present, and it usually drains into the coronary sinus.

The posterior interventricular artery, also called the posterior descending artery, runs down the groove on the back of the heart that separates the ventricles, towards the apex. It supplies the back third of the interventricular septum (the muscular wall between the ventricles) and the back walls of both ventricles. In most people it arises from the right coronary artery and lies beside the middle cardiac vein on the back of the heart. Blockage of this artery is a common cause of an inferior heart attack.

The posterior vein of the left ventricle is a vein of the heart that drains the lower (diaphragmatic) wall of the left ventricle, the surface that rests on the diaphragm. It runs over the lower surface of the left ventricle and joins the coronary sinus, the large venous channel in the groove between the atria and ventricles at the back of the heart. In a dissection it is recognised as a fine vein lying in the fat on the lower surface of the left ventricle.

A tributary of the posterior vein of the left ventricle is a small vein that joins its parent vessel on the lower surface of the left ventricle. It drains a small area of the lower left ventricular wall and carries the blood towards the coronary sinus, the main venous channel on the back of the heart. In a dissection it is recognised as a fine branch joining the parent vein, lying in the fat of the lower heart surface.

The posterolateral branch of the circumflex artery is a branch of the left circumflex coronary artery that runs over the back and side of the left ventricle. It supplies the posterolateral wall of the left ventricle, the thick outer wall that pumps blood out to the body. The circumflex artery runs in the left atrioventricular groove, so this branch is traced by following the circumflex round onto the back of the heart. Blockage of the circumflex artery can cause a lateral or posterolateral heart attack.

The right coronary artery is one of the two coronary arteries, arising from the right-hand bulge of the aortic root just above the aortic valve. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove between the right atrium and right ventricle and supplies both chambers, along with the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes in most people. Most often it also gives off the posterior interventricular artery, which runs down the back of the heart. Blockage of this artery can cause an inferior heart attack.

The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the acute margin, the sharp edge on the right side of the heart where the front and lower surfaces meet. It supplies the free wall of the right ventricle and usually continues almost to the apex. It is recognised as a branch leaving the right coronary artery in the right atrioventricular groove, and it is followed down the edge of the heart.

The right posterolateral artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that winds onto the back of the heart and supplies the back and side walls of the left ventricle. It leaves the right coronary artery as that vessel turns round the lower border of the heart, and it runs across the lower and lateral walls of the left ventricle. Blockage of this artery can cause a posterolateral heart attack.

An anterior cardiac vein is a small vein that runs up over the front of the right ventricle and drains straight into the right atrium. Unlike most cardiac veins, it does not join the coronary sinus, the main venous channel on the back of the heart, but opens into the right atrium directly. In a dissection it is seen as a thin vessel on the front of the right ventricle, leading to the right atrioventricular groove where it enters the atrium.

A diagonal artery is a branch of the left anterior descending artery that runs obliquely down and to the left across the front wall of the left ventricle. It supplies the anterior and lateral walls of the left ventricle, and it is recognised as a branch that leaves the left anterior descending artery on the front surface of the heart. Blockage of a diagonal artery can cause a heart attack affecting the front and side of the left ventricle.

An obtuse marginal artery is a branch of the left circumflex coronary artery that runs down the blunt (obtuse) left border of the heart, the rounded margin formed by the left ventricle. It supplies the lateral wall of the left ventricle and reaches towards the apex. In a dissection it is followed from the left atrioventricular groove as it turns down along the outer edge of the heart.

A septal perforator is a small branch of the left anterior descending artery that dips into the interventricular septum, the muscular wall between the two ventricles. It supplies the front two-thirds of the septum and also helps supply the bundle branches of the conduction system that run along it. These small branches can be traced back to the left anterior descending artery, which runs in the anterior interventricular groove on the front of the heart.

The sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery is a small artery that supplies the sinoatrial node, the natural pacemaker of the heart that sets the heart rate. In most people it arises from the right coronary artery near its origin and runs round to the top of the right atrium, beside the superior vena cava. It is found by tracing the right coronary artery to the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium.

The small cardiac vein is a vein of the heart that drains the right atrium and right ventricle. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove beside the right coronary artery and its marginal branch, and usually joins the coronary sinus close to its opening into the right atrium. Because it runs with the right coronary artery, it is easy to find on the surface of the heart.

A tributary of the small cardiac vein is a small vein that collects blood from the lower (inferior) wall of the right ventricle and joins its parent vein. The parent vein runs in the right atrioventricular groove, so this tributary is found in the fat near the right coronary artery on the lower surface of the heart. Look for it as a thin branch entering the parent vein.

Diagonal arteries are branches of the left anterior descending artery that cross the front of the left ventricle at a slant, running down and out towards its side wall. They supply the anterolateral part of the left ventricular wall, the part that faces forward and to the left. In a dissection, they are followed out from the left anterior descending artery, which lies in the anterior interventricular groove.

Septal perforators are small arteries that arise from the left anterior descending artery and pass through the front of the interventricular septum, the wall dividing the two ventricles. They supply the front of the septum and the bundle branches of the conduction system, which carry the electrical signal that makes the ventricles contract. On a heart section, a perforator appears as a small artery inside the septal muscle, not on the surface.

The aortic arch is the curved part of the aorta between the ascending and descending aorta, lying above the root of the left lung. It arches over the left main bronchus, and its three large branches (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries) rise from its upper surface. A fibrous cord, the ligamentum arteriosum, runs from its underside to the left pulmonary artery and is the remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus.

The ascending aorta is the short first part of the aorta, leaving the left ventricle at the aortic valve and running up behind the sternum. The root of the ascending aorta bulges at the three sinuses of Valsalva, and the left and right coronary arteries arise from these sinuses just above the valve. The pulmonary trunk lies to its left and in front, and the superior vena cava lies to its right, which helps identify it in a dissection.

The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch, arising from its upper surface and running up and to the right. It passes behind the right sternoclavicular joint and divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries, which supply the right side of the head, neck and arm. The left brachiocephalic vein crosses in front of it, which is a useful landmark in a dissection.

The descending (thoracic) aorta is the part of the aorta that runs down from the aortic arch through the posterior mediastinum, the central compartment behind the heart. It lies on the front of the vertebral column, to the left of the oesophagus, and gives off paired intercostal and bronchial branches. It passes through the aortic hiatus in the diaphragm to become the abdominal aorta.

The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium. It forms at about the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra from the union of the two common iliac veins, and runs up the right side of the abdomen behind the liver, receiving the hepatic veins that drain the liver. It passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm and opens into the lower, back part of the right atrium.

The left brachiocephalic vein, also called the left innominate vein, is formed behind the left sternoclavicular joint by the union of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. It runs obliquely to the right across the front of the upper mediastinum, passing in front of the great branches of the aortic arch, to join the right brachiocephalic vein. Where the two meet, they form the superior vena cava.

The left common carotid artery arises from the upper surface of the aortic arch, between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left subclavian artery. It ascends into the neck, lateral to the trachea and oesophagus, and divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into the external and internal carotid arteries. In the neck it lies in the carotid sheath alongside the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve.

The left inferior pulmonary vein is one of the veins that carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. It drains the lower lobe of the left lung, running forwards from the lung root in front of the descending aorta to reach the back of the left atrium. Its opening lies on the back wall of the left atrium, below the left superior pulmonary vein.

The left pulmonary artery is the branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries deoxygenated blood to the left lung. It arches over the left main bronchus to enter the hilum of the left lung, where it divides into lobar branches. It is shorter than the right pulmonary artery, and a fibrous cord called the ligamentum arteriosum, the remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, links it to the aortic arch.

The left subclavian artery is the last of the three branches of the aortic arch, arising from its upper surface just behind and to the left of the left common carotid artery. It arches over the top of the left lung, passes behind the anterior scalene muscle, and becomes the axillary artery at the outer edge of the first rib. It supplies the left arm, and it gives off the vertebral and internal thoracic arteries on its way.

The left superior pulmonary vein is one of the veins that carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. It drains the upper lobe of the left lung and the lingula, the tongue-like part of the upper lobe that corresponds to the right middle lobe. It opens into the left atrium close to the base of the left auricle, the small ear-shaped pouch on the atrium.

The pulmonary trunk is the short, wide artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It leaves the right ventricle at the pulmonary valve, runs up and back to the left of the ascending aorta, and divides beneath the aortic arch into the left and right pulmonary arteries. It is recognised in a dissection as the large vessel leaving the front of the heart, behind the sternum.

The right brachiocephalic vein, also called the right innominate vein, is formed behind the right sternoclavicular joint by the union of the right internal jugular and right subclavian veins. It runs almost straight down behind the right side of the sternum and joins the left brachiocephalic vein to form the superior vena cava. It is short and vertical, and central venous catheters inserted from the right neck or arm often pass through it into the heart.

The right inferior pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood from the lower lobe of the right lung to the left atrium. It passes behind the right atrium on its way to the back of the left atrium, and like the other pulmonary veins it has no valves. Its opening lies on the back wall of the left atrium, below the right superior pulmonary vein.

The right pulmonary artery is the branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries deoxygenated blood to the right lung. It is longer than the left branch and runs horizontally to the right, passing behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava and in front of the right main bronchus. At the root of the lung it divides into branches for the upper, middle and lower lobes.

The right superior pulmonary vein is one of the four pulmonary veins that return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. It drains the upper and middle lobes of the right lung, passing behind the superior vena cava and right atrium on its way. Its wall is thinner than that of the neighbouring pulmonary artery, which helps distinguish the two vessels in a dissection.

The superior vena cava is a large, thin-walled, valveless vein that carries blood from the head, neck and upper limbs into the upper part of the right atrium. It is formed behind the right first costal cartilage by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins, and it runs down beside the ascending aorta to enter the right atrium at the level of the third costal cartilage. In a dissection it is recognised by its wide, thin-walled lumen and its position just to the right of the ascending aorta.

The left coronary cusp is one of the three half-moon-shaped flaps (semilunar cusps) of the aortic valve, lying on the left-posterior side of the aortic root. The left coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus (the bulge of the aortic wall behind each cusp) behind this cusp, which is how the cusp can be recognised at the valve. During diastole its free edge meets the other two cusps to seal the valve, so blood cannot flow back from the aorta into the left ventricle.

The non-coronary cusp is the posterior one of the three semilunar cusps of the aortic valve, lying next to the interatrial septum and the right atrium. It is named because no coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it, unlike the left and right cusps. Its base is fibrously continuous with the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve, so the two valves share tissue at this point.

The right coronary cusp is the anterior of the three semilunar cusps of the aortic valve. The right coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it and runs to the right side of the heart. In most bicuspid aortic valves, the commonest congenital heart valve abnormality, the right and left cusps are fused together.

The mitral annulus is the dense fibrous ring that surrounds the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle, and to which both mitral leaflets are attached. Its anterior part merges with the aortic valve ring, so the two valves share fibrous tissue. The annulus gives the valve its shape, but when the left ventricle dilates the ring widens and blood can leak back into the left atrium (mitral regurgitation).

The anterior (aortic) leaflet of the mitral valve is the taller, more mobile of the two mitral leaflets, hanging from the anterior part of the annulus into the left ventricle. It occupies about one-third of the annulus and is continuous with the aortic valve, linking it to the left and non-coronary aortic cusps. During systole its free edge closes against the posterior leaflet, which stops blood flowing back into the left atrium.

The chordae tendineae of the anterolateral papillary muscle are fine, tough, tendon-like cords (the 'heart strings') running from the muscle tip to the free edges of both mitral leaflets. They hold the leaflets closed during ventricular systole, so blood cannot leak back into the left atrium. In a dissection they look white and glistening, and are much thinner than the muscular papillary tip they arise from.

The anterolateral papillary muscle is one of the two papillary muscles of the left ventricle, a cone-shaped column of heart muscle projecting into the cavity from the anterolateral wall. Its tip gives attachment to chordae tendineae running to both mitral leaflets. It contracts with the ventricle to tense these cords, holding the leaflets closed so they do not prolapse into the left atrium. In a section it appears as a thick, rounded muscular knob on the lateral wall of the cavity.

The posterior (mural) leaflet of the mitral valve is the wider of the two mitral leaflets, attached to about two-thirds of the annulus and hanging against the posterior wall of the left ventricle. Its free edge is divided by notches into three scallops, named P1 to P3. It is the leaflet most often involved in mitral valve prolapse, particularly at the middle scallop (P2).

The chordae tendineae of the posteromedial papillary muscle are the tendinous 'heart strings' that run from the tip of this muscle, on the posterior wall of the left ventricle, to the free edges of both mitral leaflets. They stop the leaflets bulging back into the left atrium during systole. In a dissection they look white and thread-like, and can be followed from the valve edge down to the muscle tip.

The posteromedial papillary muscle is one of the two papillary muscles of the left ventricle, arising from the posterior wall of the ventricle close to the septum. Its tip gives attachment to chordae tendineae that run to both mitral leaflets, and its contraction during systole helps keep the valve closed. It is usually supplied by a single coronary artery, which makes it more vulnerable to ischaemia (a shortage of blood supply) than the anterolateral muscle.

The anterior cusp of the pulmonary valve is one of the three semilunar cusps that guard the opening from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk. It is the front cusp of the valve, while the left and right cusps lie behind it. Its edges meet the other two cusps when the valve closes in diastole, which stops blood flowing back into the right ventricle.

The left cusp of the pulmonary valve is one of the three semilunar cusps, lying on the left-posterior side of the valve ring where the right ventricle opens into the pulmonary trunk. It is a thin, pocket-shaped flap that is pressed against its neighbours when the valve closes, sealing the opening. When the pulmonary trunk is opened, it is the cusp on the patient's left, next to the anterior cusp.

The right cusp of the pulmonary valve is one of the three semilunar cusps, lying on the right-posterior side of the valve ring at the top of the right ventricular outflow tract. Its free edge has a small thickened nodule at its centre (the nodule of Arantius), which helps the cusps meet and seal the valve. In an opened pulmonary trunk it is the cusp on the patient's right, next to the anterior cusp.

The tricuspid annulus is the fibrous ring surrounding the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle, to which the three leaflets of the tricuspid valve are attached. It is less dense and less distinct than the mitral annulus. When the right ventricle dilates, the ring widens and the valve may leak back into the right atrium (tricuspid regurgitation).

The chordae tendineae of the anterior papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve are fine tendinous cords that run from the tip of this muscle, on the anterior wall of the right ventricle, to the anterior and posterior leaflets. They hold these leaflets closed during right ventricular systole, so blood cannot leak back into the right atrium. In an opened ventricle they appear as thread-like strands fanning out from the muscle tip.

The anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve is the largest of its three leaflets, lying over the front wall of the right ventricle towards the outflow tract. During systole its free edge closes against the septal and posterior leaflets, stopping blood flowing back into the right atrium. Its chordae come mainly from the anterior and septal papillary muscles, and in an opened ventricle it is the broad flap nearest the outflow tract.

The anterior papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve is one of the three papillary muscles of the right ventricle, usually the largest, arising from the anterior wall of the ventricle. Its tip gives attachment to chordae tendineae that run to the anterior and posterior leaflets. As the ventricle contracts it tenses these cords, so the leaflets close without bulging back into the right atrium.

The chordae tendineae of the posterior papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve are fine, tough cords that link the tip of this muscle, which arises from the inferior (posterior) wall of the right ventricle, to the posterior and septal leaflets. They keep these leaflets from bulging back into the right atrium during right ventricular systole. They are best seen in an opened ventricle as white threads running from the muscle tip to the leaflet edges.

The posterior (inferior) leaflet of the tricuspid valve is attached to the posterior-inferior part of the annulus, lying against the inferior wall of the right ventricle. Its free edge meets the anterior and septal leaflets during systole, and its chordae come from the posterior and anterior papillary muscles. In an opened right ventricle it is the flap sitting between the anterior and septal leaflets along the inferior wall.

The posterior papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve is one of the three papillary muscles of the right ventricle, a cone-shaped projection from the posterior (inferior) wall of the ventricle. Its tip gives rise to chordae tendineae that run to the posterior and septal leaflets. Its contraction during systole keeps these leaflets from prolapsing back into the right atrium.

The chordae tendineae of the septal papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve are fine, tendinous cords that run from the tip of this muscle, which arises from the interventricular septum, to the septal and anterior leaflets. They tether these leaflets so that they close fully during right ventricular systole. In a dissection they can be seen as delicate white threads on the septal side of the ventricle.

The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve is the medial leaflet, attached to the interventricular septum. Its free edge meets the anterior and posterior leaflets during systole to prevent backflow into the right atrium, and its chordae come from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. The atrioventricular node and bundle lie close to its base, in the triangle of Koch, a small area of the right atrium beside the septum, so surgery here risks heart block.

The septal papillary muscle of the tricuspid valve is one of the three papillary muscles of the right ventricle, arising from the interventricular septum. Its tip gives rise to chordae tendineae that run to the septal and anterior leaflets. In a section it appears as a muscular projection from the septum into the cavity, on the medial side of the ventricle.

The sinoatrial (SA) node is a small cluster of specialised pacemaker cells in the wall of the right atrium, at its junction with the superior vena cava. It generates the electrical impulse that starts each heartbeat, at about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest, and spreads it through the atrial muscle. In histology, nodal cells are paler and have fewer myofibrils than the surrounding atrial muscle fibres, so they are recognised by their pale, loosely arranged appearance.

The anterior internodal pathway is a band of specialised atrial muscle that carries the electrical impulse from the sinoatrial node across the front of the right atrium towards the atrioventricular node. It is one of three internodal tracts that conduct faster than the surrounding atrial muscle. Its branch, Bachmann bundle, carries the impulse on into the left atrium.

The middle internodal pathway is one of the three tracts of specialised atrial muscle that run from the sinoatrial node to the atrioventricular node, lying between the anterior and posterior tracts in the right atrial wall. Like the others, it conducts the impulse faster than the surrounding atrial muscle, so the atria are activated in an orderly sequence. Its course is mapped mainly by electrophysiological studies rather than seen in a dissection.

The posterior internodal pathway is one of the three tracts of specialised atrial muscle carrying the impulse from the sinoatrial node to the atrioventricular node. It runs back along the posterior wall of the right atrium, close to the crista terminalis and the opening of the coronary sinus, to reach the posterior part of the AV node. Its faster conduction is what distinguishes it from the ordinary atrial muscle around it.

Bachmann bundle is the band of atrial muscle that carries the electrical impulse from the right atrium into the left atrium, crossing the upper front part of the interatrial septum. It starts from the anterior internodal pathway near the right atrial appendage and runs to the left atrial appendage, so that both atria contract almost together. It is recognised by this course across the roof of the atria between the two appendages.

The atrioventricular (AV) node is a small mass of specialised cardiac muscle cells in the floor of the right atrium, within the triangle of Koch, a small triangular area near the opening of the coronary sinus and the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve. It receives the impulse from the sinoatrial node and holds it back briefly, so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles begin. Its cells are smaller and paler than working myocardium, with few myofibrils, which helps identify it on a histology slide.

The atrioventricular (AV) bundle, or bundle of His, is the only normal electrical link between the atria and the ventricles. It leaves the AV node, passes through the central fibrous body, and divides at the top of the muscular interventricular septum into the right and left bundle branches. It is named after the anatomist Wilhelm His, and its position at the top of the septum helps locate it in a dissection.

The central fibrous body is a dense knot of collagenous connective tissue at the centre of the heart, where the mitral, tricuspid and aortic valve rings meet. It is the thickest part of the fibrous skeleton, which electrically insulates the atrial muscle from the ventricular muscle, so the only normal route between them is the atrioventricular bundle that passes through it. In a dissection it looks like a firm, white fibrous knot lying behind the root of the aorta.

The septomarginal trabecula, also called the moderator band, is a muscular ridge that crosses the cavity of the right ventricle from the lower interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch of the conduction system across the ventricle, so that the impulse reaches the anterior papillary muscle and the front wall of the right ventricle. In a dissection it is a free, rounded cord of muscle that stands out on the inner surface of the right ventricle.

The right bundle branch is a cord of specialised conducting fibres that continues from the bundle of His down the right side of the interventricular septum. It runs through the septomarginal trabecula to the anterior papillary muscle, then spreads over the free wall of the right ventricle. Its fibres are larger and paler than working cardiac muscle and rich in glycogen, which helps identify them on a histology slide.

The left bundle branch is the continuation of the bundle of His that supplies the left ventricle. It runs down the left side of the interventricular septum just beneath the endocardium, then splits into the left anterior and left posterior fascicles. Damage to it widens the QRS complex on an electrocardiogram, because the left ventricle is then activated more slowly.

The left anterior fascicle is the thin, ribbon-like front division of the left bundle branch. It spreads across the upper front part of the left ventricular septum to reach the anterolateral papillary muscle and the anterior wall of the left ventricle. Damage to it shifts the QRS axis to the left on an electrocardiogram.

The left posterior fascicle is the broad, short posterior division of the left bundle branch. It fans out over the lower posterior part of the left ventricular septum to reach the posteromedial papillary muscle. It has a dual blood supply from the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries, so it is less often damaged than the anterior fascicle.

Purkinje fibres are the terminal branches of the conduction system, which spread the impulse from the bundle branches into the working myocardium. In the left ventricle they lie just beneath the endocardium on the septal and free-wall surfaces, so contraction starts near the apex and spreads upward. Under the microscope they are large, pale cells with glycogen-rich cytoplasm and few myofibrils lying at the edges.

The right ventricular Purkinje fibres are the terminal branches of the right bundle branch, spreading over the right side of the septum, the moderator band and the free wall of the right ventricle. They lie just beneath the endocardium and relay the impulse to the working myocardium, so the right ventricle contracts from the apex upward. They are recognised by their size and pale staining, as large cells with glycogen-rich cytoplasm and peripheral myofibrils.

The fibrous pericardium is the outer, strong layer of the pericardial sac, made of dense collagenous connective tissue. It limits overdistension of the heart, and below it is fused with the central tendon of the diaphragm, while above it blends with the walls of the great vessels, so it anchors the heart in the mediastinum. In a dissection it is a tough, white, opaque sheath that must be opened to reach the serous pericardium beneath.

The parietal layer of the serous pericardium is the thin, glistening inner lining of the fibrous pericardium. It is a single layer of flat mesothelial cells (simple squamous epithelium) resting on a thin connective-tissue base. At the roots of the great vessels it turns back on itself to become the visceral layer on the heart, so the two form one continuous sac around the pericardial cavity.

The visceral layer of the serous pericardium, also called the epicardium, is the thin serous membrane that forms the outer surface of the heart and of the roots of the great vessels. It consists of flat mesothelial cells on loose connective tissue carrying the coronary vessels and fat. In a dissection, its smooth, glistening surface is what is seen on the heart once the fibrous and parietal layers have been removed.

The central tendon of the diaphragm is a broad, flat, non-contractile sheet of dense fibrous tissue at the centre of the diaphragm's dome. Muscle fibres from the rim of the diaphragm, arising from the lower ribs, sternum and lumbar spine, converge on it, so their contraction flattens the dome during inspiration. Its upper surface is fused with the fibrous pericardium, which is why the heart rests on it.

The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle cells that contract to pump blood. It lies between the epicardium outside and the endocardium inside, and it is far thicker in the left ventricle than in the atria. Under the microscope the cardiac muscle fibres are striated and branched, with central nuclei and intercalated discs that join neighbouring cells end to end.

The endocardium is the thin inner lining of the heart chambers and valves, the layer that comes into direct contact with the blood. It consists of a single layer of flat endothelial cells on a thin layer of connective tissue containing elastic fibres, and it is continuous with the lining of the great vessels. In a histology slide, look for a thin row of flat endothelial nuclei facing the lumen, resting on the myocardium.

keys: Epicardial connective tissue and fat (wall block)
parts.description: The epicardial connective tissue and fat is the loose connective tissue and adipose tissue lying beneath the epicardium on the outer surface of the heart. It supports the coronary arteries and veins as they run over the surface, and it is thickest along the atrioventricular and interventricular grooves where the large coronary vessels lie. In a dissection it appears as yellow fat packed around the coronary vessels, most visible in these grooves.

keys: Visceral layer of serous pericardium (epicardium) (wall block)
parts.description: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium is the outermost layer of the heart wall, the thin, moist membrane that forms the heart's outer surface, with the coronary vessels and epicardial fat lying just beneath it. It is continuous with the parietal layer where the great vessels leave the heart, and it borders the pericardial cavity. Under the microscope it appears as a flat sheet of mesothelial cells lining the outer surface of the myocardium.

keys: Pericardial cavity with pericardial fluid (wall block)
parts.description: The pericardial cavity is the narrow potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium. It normally holds a small amount of clear serous fluid that lubricates the two surfaces, so the heart beats with little friction. Excess fluid or blood collecting here can compress the heart, a condition called cardiac tamponade.

keys: Parietal layer of serous pericardium (wall block)
parts.description: The parietal layer of the serous pericardium lies on the inner face of the fibrous pericardium and forms the lining of the pericardial sac. It is a smooth, moist membrane of mesothelium, so the two layers of the sac glide over each other as the heart beats. Together with the visceral layer, it encloses the pericardial cavity.

The fibrous pericardium is the outer, protective wall of the pericardial sac, made of tough, dense collagen fibres with few cells. It is attached to the diaphragm below, to the great vessels above, and to the sternum in front by the sternopericardial ligaments, so it holds the heart in place in the middle of the chest. In a dissection it is the most external layer of the pericardium, tough and white.

A coronary artery branch is a small twig of the left or right coronary artery that runs over the heart surface in the epicardial fat before entering the myocardium. These branches carry oxygenated blood to the heart muscle, and occlusion of one causes infarction of the region it supplies. In a histology slide they are muscular arteries with a thick smooth muscle wall, a round lumen and an endothelial lining.

A cardiac vein is a small vein that runs in the epicardial fat beside the coronary arteries, collecting blood from the heart muscle. Most of these veins drain into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium near the tricuspid valve. Their walls are thinner than those of arteries of similar size, with a wider, less rounded lumen, which helps identify them on a histology slide.

The trabeculae carneae are the irregular muscular ridges and columns on the inner surface of the ventricles. They are formed of myocardium lined by endocardium, which gives the ventricular wall its rough, ridged inner surface. They are especially coarse near the apex, where they stand out as fleshy bars across the cavity.

Purkinje fibres in the ventricular wall form the subendocardial network that receives the impulse from the bundle branches. They pass the signal to the working myocardium through specialised junctions, so the whole ventricle contracts in a coordinated sweep from the apex upward. Histologically they are large, pale-staining cells whose cytoplasm is rich in glycogen, with the myofibrils pushed to the cell edge.

The right atrial wall is the thin wall of the right atrium, made of an inner endocardium, a middle layer of thin atrial myocardium, and an outer epicardium carrying fat and coronary vessels. It is much thinner than the ventricular wall, and its inner surface is smooth behind the crista terminalis but ridged by pectinate muscles in front. The right atrium is recognised in a dissection by this thin wall and its ear-shaped auricle.

The atrial endocardium is the thin lining of the atria, made of flat endothelial cells on a thin connective-tissue layer. It is continuous with the lining of the ventricles at the atrioventricular valves. It is smooth over the posterior wall of the right atrium but is raised into ridges over the pectinate muscles in the front of the atrium and in the auricles.

The atrial epicardium is the outer layer of the atrial wall, a thin sheet of flat mesothelial cells over loose connective tissue that carries small coronary vessels and fat. It is continuous with the serous pericardium at the roots of the great veins that enter the atria. In a dissection, the epicardial fat is most visible in the groove between the atria and ventricles, where the coronary sinus runs.

The crista terminalis is a vertical muscular ridge on the inner wall of the right atrium, running from the opening of the superior vena cava to the opening of the inferior vena cava. It separates the smooth-walled posterior part of the atrium, which develops from the sinus venosus, from the rough anterior part with the pectinate muscles. The sinoatrial node lies beneath the epicardium at its upper end, so the ridge is a useful landmark.

The pectinate muscles are the parallel, comb-like ridges of myocardium that project from the inner wall of the right atrial auricle and the front of the atrium. Each ridge is lined by endocardium, and in the left atrium they are found only inside the left auricle. In a dissection the name is easy to remember, because pecten is Latin for comb.
